extracted.intended_audience: newsroom leaders, editors, social media managers and journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for newsrooms on drafting, testing, approving, and implementing or updating social media policies for institutional and individual staff accounts. Emphasizes governance, scope, boundary-testing, and regular review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with the why
rubrics_metrics.description: State (in words that can be shared company-wide) the newsroom’s goals for having any social media presence. Use specific examples, even platform-specific examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be specific about what the organization wants to achieve (establish/expand brand, acquire audience, connect with subscribers, engagement, be at center of community conversation). Prioritize the value of different goals. Example given: 'The Scoop is on many different social platforms to introduce our work to new audiences, to participate in the important conversations of the day and to hear from those that we serve.' The page notes many policies skip this step and only say vague goals like 'We need to go where the audience is.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Commit leadership, time, and diverse input
rubrics_metrics.description: Designate a manager or team with the clout and journalism leadership skills to facilitate difficult conversations and include many voices in the revision process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Updating policies is tedious, tense and time-consuming; require dedicated leadership to get buy-in. Seek input from a diverse group of advisers or a small committee to ensure different beliefs and perspectives are represented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish institutional account governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Define who can create institutional accounts, who manages passwords, who determines goals and voice, how accounts are retired, and where knowledge is archived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with institutional accounts before individual presence. Record and archive account information so knowledge isn't lost. Clarify retirement procedures and password management to maintain security and continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulate how social media strategies should develop
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a process for how strategies will be set and evolve, including who determines goals/voice and how decisions are reviewed over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include specifics about development of strategy at institutional and individual levels. Example: reporters should discuss platform choices with editors and review goals during annual evaluations. The policy should say whether staff are expected or required to participate and on which platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define expectations for individual professional presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify whether journalists or staff are expected to be on social media, and if so, why, what platforms, and how that fits into job responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give beat-specific guidance (e.g., political reporters may use Twitter for tips; education reporters may use TikTok; outdoors reporters may use Instagram). If social media is part of job description, discuss details with managers and review during performance evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delineate who counts as a public representative of the newsroom
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify who on staff should be considered publicly identifiable representatives (usually folks with bylines, supervisors of those with bylines, and senior management) and what is expected of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representatives should comport themselves as if representing the company; behaviors that undermine the newsroom's values are subject to reprimand. This helps set boundaries and clarifies responsibilities for visible staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set rules about political expression and narrow exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify whether public-facing journalists and senior leaders should keep political views private (e.g., not endorsing candidates or weighing in on public policy), while clarifying permissible advocacy such as support for human rights causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidance includes two example approaches: (1) representatives are expected to keep political views private and not endorse candidates, and (2) an alternative that prohibits endorsements but allows support for causes like marriage equality or Black Lives Matter. For thorny topics (e.g., abortion), recommend case-by-case discussions with managers rather than blanket prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit abusive conduct and hateful speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Remind staff that social media is a public space and certain behaviors—name-calling, openly attacking colleagues, racist, misogynistic or other reprehensible speech—are always subject to reprimand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize that even private accounts are effectively public and that policies must address unacceptable conduct. This criterion is part of boundary-setting when testing the draft policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test the draft policy and explore boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: After drafting, pilot or test the policy to explore edge cases and discover what behaviors or scenarios are in or out of scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use testing to delineate what is permissible (e.g., sharing personal experiences with political implications) and to surface issues requiring managerial judgment. Testing helps avoid vague or unenforceable rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a small review committee with clear chair and cadence
rubrics_metrics.description: Form a committee with representatives from key areas, assign a chair, and convene at least quarterly to review the policy and consider trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committee should be called for advice on trends (not individual personnel cases). Regular review ensures policy keeps pace with platform changes and newsroom needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure approval, follow-through, and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan for final adoption and implementation: obtain buy-in from publisher/board, have HR and legal review, introduce policy to staff, and ensure managers can onboard employees to the standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify an influential advocate to shepherd the policy through administrative black holes. Once adopted, distribute by memo, hold workshops or department discussions, and make managers responsible for enforcing and teaching the policy. Failure to follow through risks the policy being ignored and creating a dangerous ethical climate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish policy-level guidance from individual case handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify that the policy/committee addresses trends and standards, while supervisors or HR handle individual violations or personnel matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using the policy body to adjudicate single-person disputes; reserve operational enforcement and disciplinary measures for supervisors/HR to ensure due process and appropriate handling.
